claims.evidence: This is a conceptual statement about the two modeling approaches used in the study.

claims.claim: RL models assume that belief updating is proportional to the estimation error.
claims.source: The RL models assume that belief updating is proportional to the estimation error.
claims.evidence: This describes a fundamental assumption of the RL modeling approach.

claims.claim: The COVID-19 pandemic represented a chronic adverse life context, drastically altering individual and social realities.
claims.source: The COVID-19 pandemic represented a chronic adverse life context, drastically altering individual and social realities.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the nature of the COVID-19 pandemic based on common knowledge.

claims.claim: Stress, anxiety, and depression have increased during the pandemic.
claims.source: The existing literature documenting the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the associated changes in everyday life on mental health has shown that stress, anxiety, and depression have increased during the pandemic (Rajkumar, 2020; World Health Organization, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Belief updating during reversal learning became more erratic and was linked to a rise in paranoia during the COVID-19 pandemic across the US.
claims.source: Moreover, previous work has demonstrated that belief updating during reversal learning became more erratic and was linked to a rise in paranoia during the COVID-19 pandemic across the US (Suthaharan et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Optimism biases are beneficial in exploratory behavior, reduce stress, and improve mental and physical health and well-being.
claims.source: The optimism biases are beneficial in exploratory behavior, reduce stress, and improve mental and physical health and well-being (Taylor and Brown, 1988; Scheier et al., 1994; Scheier et al., 2001; Boehm and Lyubomirsky, 2008; Carver et al., 2010; Carver and Scheier, 2014; Boehm et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The benefits of optimism biases promote resilience, which is especially important for fitness and survival during a pandemic.
claims.source: These benefits promote resilience, which is especially important for fitness and survival during a pandemic (Berger-Tal and Avgar, 2012; McKay and Dennett, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Optimism biases can lead to suboptimal decision-making.
claims.source: On the contrary, optimism biases can lead to suboptimal decision-making.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the potential negative consequences of optimism biases.

claims.claim: Contextual factors such as acute stress, perceived threat, and depression have been shown to reduce or even reverse optimistically biased belief updating.
claims.source: Contextual factors such as acute stress, perceived threat, and depression have been shown to reduce or even reverse optimistically biased belief updating (Strunk et al., 2006; Garrett et al., 2014; Korn et al., 2014; Garrett et al., 2018; Kuper-Smith et al., 2020; Czekalla et al., 2021; Bottemanne et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: 58 participants were tested outside the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, either in October 2019 (n=30) or in June 2022 (n=28).
claims.source: Among them, 58 participants were tested outside the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, either in October 2019, 3 months before the outbreak in France (n=30) or 2 years after in June 2022 (n=28), after the lift of the sanitary state of emergency.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample composition.

claims.claim: 65 participants were tested during the sanitary state of emergency due to the COVID-19 outbreak in France.
claims.source: Their belief updating behavior was compared to 65 participants tested during the sanitary state of emergency due to the COVID-19 outbreak in France.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample composition.

claims.claim: 34 participants were tested during the first very strict lockdown from March to April 2020.
claims.source: This was either during the first very strict lockdown of social and economic life (e.g. schools closed, stay-at-home orders, shops, and museums closed) from March to April 2020 (n=34) or 1 year later in May 2021 (n=31), when lockdown was less strict (e.g. schools open, museums and shops closed, part-time curfew), but the COVID-19 pandemic was still unfolding.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample composition.

claims.claim: 31 participants were tested in May 2021 when lockdown was less strict.
claims.source: This was either during the first very strict lockdown of social and economic life (e.g. schools closed, stay-at-home orders, shops, and museums closed) from March to April 2020 (n=34) or 1 year later in May 2021 (n=31), when lockdown was less strict (e.g. schools open, museums and shops closed, part-time curfew), but the COVID-19 pandemic was still unfolding.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample composition.

claims.claim: A linear mixed effects model found a significant interaction estimation error valence by context (ß=–5.54, SE = 1.69, t(232) = –3.28, p=0.001, 95% CI [-8.87 to –2.21]).
claims.source: The model found a significant interaction estimation error valence by context (ß=–5.54, SE = 1.69, t(232) = –3.28, p=0.001, 95% CI [-8.87 to –2.21]; Appendix 7—table 2), which holds when further controlling for the distance variable (Appendix 7—table 3).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear mixed effects model analysis.

claims.claim: The power of the interaction effect was 75% leaving a 25% risk for type II errors.
claims.source: The power of this effect was 75% leaving a 25% risk for type II errors.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the post-hoc power analysis.

claims.claim: Optimistically biased belief updating disappeared during the COVID-19 pandemic compared to participants tested outside the pandemic.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1a and b, optimistically biased belief updating disappeared during the COVID-19 pandemic compared to participants tested outside the pandemic.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on observed belief updating behavior and shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Optimistically biased belief updating was decreased among participants tested during the initial COVID-19-related strict lockdown in March and April 2020 compared to those tested before the outbreak in October 2019 (EE valence by context 1: ß=–7.39, SE = 2.29, t(228) = –3.21, p=0.002, 95% CI [-11.91 to –2.86]).
claims.source: More specifically, it was decreased among participants tested during the initial COVID-19-related strict lockdown in March and April 2020 (EE valence by context 1: ß=–7.39, SE = 2.29, t(228) = –3.21, p=0.002, 95% CI [-11.91 to –2.86]; Appendix 7—table 4), as well as in May 2021 (EE valence by context 2: ß=–5.59, SE = 2.36, t(228) = –2.37, p=0.02, 95% CI [-10.24 to –0.93]; Appendix 7—table 4), compared to those tested before the outbreak in October 2019, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear mixed effects model analysis.

claims.claim: Optimistically biased belief updating was decreased among participants tested in May 2021 compared to those tested before the outbreak in October 2019 (EE valence by context 2: ß=–5.59, SE = 2.36, t(228) = –2.37, p=0.02, 95% CI [-10.24 to –0.93]).
claims.source: More specifically, it was decreased among participants tested during the initial COVID-19-related strict lockdown in March and April 2020 (EE valence by context 1: ß=–7.39, SE = 2.29, t(228) = –3.21, p=0.002, 95% CI [-11.91 to –2.86]; Appendix 7—table 4), as well as in May 2021 (EE valence by context 2: ß=–5.59, SE = 2.36, t(228) = –2.37, p=0.02, 95% CI [-10.24 to –0.93]; Appendix 7—table 4), compared to those tested before the outbreak in October 2019, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear mixed effects model analysis.

claims.claim: The bias re-emerged among participants tested one year later at the time of the lift of the sanitary state of emergency in June 2022, returning to levels akin to those observed before the pandemic in October 2019 (EE valence by context 3: ß=–2.11, SE = 2.46, t(228) = –0.86, p=0.39, 95% CI [-6.95 to 2.73]).
claims.source: The bias re-emerged among participants tested one year later at the time of the lift of the sanitary state of emergency in June 2022, returning to levels akin to those observed before the pandemic in October 2019 (EE valence by context 3: ß=–2.11, SE = 2.46, t(228) = –0.86, p=0.39, 95% CI [-6.95 to 2.73]; Figure 1a, Appendix 7—table 4).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear mixed effects model analysis and shown in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: The effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on belief updating was driven by a significant decrease in belief updating following good news during the pandemic compared to participants tested outside the pandemic (t(121) = 2.66, p=0.009, Cohen's d=0.48).
claims.source: The effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on belief updating was driven by a significant decrease in belief updating following good news during the pandemic compared to participants tested outside the pandemic (t(121) = 2.66, p=0.009, Cohen's d=0.48, two-sampled, two-tailed t-test, Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the t-test analysis and shown in Figure 1b.

claims.claim: No contextual group difference was observed for belief updating following bad news (t(121) = –1.77, p=0.08, Cohen's d=–0.32).
claims.source: No contextual group difference was observed for belief updating following bad news (t(121) = –1.77, p=0.08, Cohen's d=–0.32, two-sampled, two-tailed t-test, Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the t-test analysis and shown in Figure 1b.

claims.claim: The effect could be reproduced when fitting an analogous LME to belief updates observed in the group of participants (n=28) who were tested both before and during the pandemic (EE valence by context interaction: ß=–7.66, SE = 1.49, t(103) = –5.13, p=1.35e-06, 95% CI [-10.62 to -4.70]).
claims.source: This effect could be reproduced when fitting an analogous LME to belief updates observed in the group of participants (n=28) who were tested both before and during the pandemic (EE valence by context interaction: ß=–7.66, SE = 1.49, t(103) = –5.13, p=1.35e-06, 95% CI [-10.62 to -4.70]; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Appendix 7—table 5, Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the within-subject analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: When categorizing trials as good or bad news based on an alternative EE calculation, the context-by-EE valence interaction remained significant.
claims.source: Moreover, previous studies of optimistically biased belief updating calculated the estimation error (EE) on the difference between the estimate for someone else (eBR) and the base rate (BR), following: EE = eBR - BR (Kuzmanovic et al., 2018; Kuzmanovic and Rigoux, 2017; Garrett and Sharot, 2014; Kuzmanovic et al., 2015). When categorizing trials as good or bad news based on this alternative EE calculation, the context-by-EE valence interaction remained significant (Appendix 7—table 6).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from an alternative analysis approach.

claims.claim: Experiencing the COVID-19 pandemic influenced participants' confidence in the base rates, with significantly lower confidence ratings observed among those tested outside the pandemic compared to those tested during it (ß=14.11, SE = 4.52, t(233) = 3.12, p=0.002, 95% CI [5.19 to 23.02]).
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1c, experiencing the COVID-19 pandemic influenced participants' confidence in the base rates, with significantly lower confidence ratings observed among those tested outside the pandemic compared to those tested during it (ß=14.11, SE = 4.52, t(233) = 3.12, p=0.002, 95% CI [5.19 to 23.02]; Appendix 7—table 7).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear mixed effects model analysis and shown in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: A significant interaction of EE valence by context was found for absolute estimation error magnitude (ß=2.19, SE = 0.67, t(233) = 3.28, p=0.001, 95% CI [0.88 to 3.51]).
claims.source: Moreover, a significant interaction of EE valence by context (ß=2.19, SE = 0.67, t(233) = 3.28, p=0.001, 95% CI [0.88 to 3.51]; Appendix 7—table 8) was found for absolute estimation error magnitude.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear mixed effects model analysis.

claims.claim: Participants tested during the pandemic overestimated their risk of experiencing adverse future life events relative to base rates more largely than participants tested outside the pandemic (t(121) = –3.01, p=0.003, Cohen's d=–0.54).
claims.source: This finding indicated that participants tested during the pandemic overestimated their risk of experiencing adverse future life events relative to base rates more largely than participants tested outside the pandemic (t(121) = –3.01, p=0.003, Cohen's d=–0.54, Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the t-test analysis and shown in Figure 1d.

claims.claim: The two groups did not differ significantly in the magnitude of negative estimation errors (t(121) = –0.49, p=0.63, Cohen's d=–0.09).
claims.source: On the contrary, the two groups did not differ significantly in the magnitude of negative estimation errors (i.e. initial underestimations relative to base rates; t(121) = –0.49, p=0.63, Cohen's d=–0.09, two-sampled, two-tailed t-tests; Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the t-test analysis and shown in Figure 1d.

claims.claim: Participants tested during the pandemic overestimated less frequently than participants tested outside the pandemic (t(121) = 2.40, p=0.02, Cohen's d=0.43).
claims.source: Participants tested during the pandemic overestimated less frequently than participants tested outside the pandemic (t(121) = 2.40, p=0.02, Cohen's d=0.43, two-sampled, two-tailed t-test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the t-test analysis.

claims.claim: No significant difference between groups was found for the frequency of underestimations (t(121) = –1.85, p=0.07, Cohen's d=–0.33).
claims.source: No significant difference between groups was found for the frequency of underestimations (i.e. reflected by the number of bad news trials; t(121) = –1.85, p=0.07, Cohen's d=–0.33, two-sampled, two-tailed t-test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the t-test analysis.

claims.claim: Participants held fewer but stronger negative future outlooks during the pandemic compared to those tested outside the pandemic.
claims.source: These results indicated that participants held fewer but stronger negative future outlooks during the pandemic compared to those tested outside the pandemic.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about estimation errors.

claims.claim: Belief updating outside the pandemic was more RL-like and optimistic (pxp = 1, Ef = 0.77).
claims.source: This approach revealed that belief updating outside the pandemic was more RL-like and optimistic (pxp = 1, Ef = 0.77), while during the pandemic, it was best explained by a rational Bayesian updating model (pxp = 0.90, Ef = 0.43; Figure 2a–c).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational modeling and model comparison analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: During the pandemic, belief updating was best explained by a rational Bayesian updating model (pxp = 0.90, Ef = 0.43).
claims.source: This approach revealed that belief updating outside the pandemic was more RL-like and optimistic (pxp = 1, Ef = 0.77), while during the pandemic, it was best explained by a rational Bayesian updating model (pxp = 0.90, Ef = 0.43; Figure 2a–c).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational modeling and model comparison analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Similar findings were obtained when conducting model comparisons in the participants tested both before and during the lockdown (n=28).
claims.source: Similar findings were obtained when conducting model comparisons in the participants tested both before and during the lockdown (n=28; Appendix 1 , Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the within-subject model comparison analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A linear mixed effects model detected a main effect of EE valence on learning rates (ß=0.09, SE = 0.01, t(236) = 7.14, p=1.18e-11, 95% CI [0.06 to 0.11]).
claims.source: A linear mixed effects model (LME), analogous to the LME fitted to observed belief updates, was fitted to the learning rates and detected a main effect of EE valence (ß=0.09, SE = 0.01, t(236) = 7.14, p=1.18e-11, 95% CI [0.06 to 0.11]; Appendix 7—table 9), and a significant interaction EE valence by context (ß=–0.03, SE = 0.02, t(236) = –2.11, p=0.04, 95% CI [-0.07 to –0.002]; Figure 3a, Appendix 7—table 9).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear mixed effects model analysis of learning rates.

claims.claim: A significant interaction EE valence by context was detected for learning rates (ß=–0.03, SE = 0.02, t(236) = –2.11, p=0.04, 95% CI [-0.07 to –0.002]).
claims.source: A linear mixed effects model (LME), analogous to the LME fitted to observed belief updates, was fitted to the learning rates and detected a main effect of EE valence (ß=0.09, SE = 0.01, t(236) = 7.14, p=1.18e-11, 95% CI [0.06 to 0.11]; Appendix 7—table 9), and a significant interaction EE valence by context (ß=–0.03, SE = 0.02, t(236) = –2.11, p=0.04, 95% CI [-0.07 to –0.002]; Figure 3a, Appendix 7—table 9).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear mixed effects model analysis of learning rates shown in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: A main effect of EE valence on learning rates was detected when comparing the participants who were tested both before and during the pandemic (ß=0.08, SE = 0.02, t(105) = 3.22, p=0.002, 95% CI [0.03 to 0.12]).
claims.source: A main effect of EE valence (ß=0.08, SE = 0.02, t(105) = 3.22, p=0.002, 95% CI [0.03 to 0.12]; Appendix 7—table 10) and context (ß=–0.10, SE = 0.03, t(105) = –3.10, p=0.003, 95% CI [-0.17 to –0.04]; Appendix 7—table 10) on learning rates was detected when comparing the participants, who were tested both before and during the pandemic.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the within-subject analysis of learning rates.

claims.claim: A main effect of context on learning rates was detected when comparing the participants who were tested both before and during the pandemic (ß=–0.10, SE = 0.03, t(105) = –3.10, p=0.003, 95% CI [-0.17 to –0.04]).
claims.source: A main effect of EE valence (ß=0.08, SE = 0.02, t(105) = 3.22, p=0.002, 95% CI [0.03 to 0.12]; Appendix 7—table 10) and context (ß=–0.10, SE = 0.03, t(105) = –3.10, p=0.003, 95% CI [-0.17 to –0.04]; Appendix 7—table 10) on learning rates was detected when comparing the participants, who were tested both before and during the pandemic.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the within-subject analysis of learning rates.

claims.claim: All participants' learning rates were lower in response to bad news than to good news.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3a, all participants' learning rates were lower in response to bad news than to good news.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the learning rate analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: The difference between good and bad news learning rates was significantly reduced for participants tested during the pandemic.
claims.source: Still, the difference between good and bad news learning rates was significantly reduced for participants tested during the pandemic.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the learning rate analysis.

claims.claim: The effect of context on the learning rates was driven by a decrease in the learning rates from positive estimation errors in participants tested during the pandemic compared to participants tested outside the pandemic (t(121) = 2.17, p=0.03, Cohen's d=0.39).
claims.source: In line with the observed belief updating after good and bad news, the effect of context on the learning rates was driven by a decrease in the learning rates from positive estimation errors in participants tested during the pandemic compared to participants tested outside the pandemic (t(121) = 2.17, p=0.03, Cohen's d=0.39, two-sampled, two-tailed t-test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the t-test analysis of learning rates.

claims.claim: Both groups did not differ in their learning rates from negative estimation errors (t(121) = 0.87, p=0.39, Cohen's d=0.16).
claims.source: Both groups did not differ in their learning rates from negative estimation errors (t(121) = 0.87, p=0.39, Cohen's d=0.16, two-sampled, two-tailed t-test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the t-test analysis of learning rates.

claims.claim: Parameter recovery was successful for the scaling (r=0.92, p<0.001) and asymmetry (r=0.82, p<0.001) components of the learning rates.
claims.source: Parameter recovery was successful for the scaling (r=0.92, p<0.001) and asymmetry (r=0.82, p<0.001) components of the learning rates (Figure 3b), which indicated that the model gave identifiable values for these parameters (parameter recovery was also conducted on each group and each model family separately, results are reported in Appendix 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the parameter recovery analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Linear mixed effects modeling found a main effect of context for the asymmetry component (ß=–0.04, SE = 0.02, t(117) = –2.32, p=0.02, 95% CI [-0.07 to –0.01]).
claims.source: Linear mixed effects modeling found a main effect of context for the asymmetry component (ß=–0.04, SE = 0.02, t(117) = –2.32, p=0.02, 95% CI [-0.07 to –0.01]; Figure 3c, Appendix 7—table 11), but not for the scaling component (ß=–0.07, SE = 0.05, t(117) = –1.54, p=0.13, 95% CI [-0.16 to 0.02]; Figure 3c, Appendix 7—table 12).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear mixed effects model analysis of learning rate components shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: Linear mixed effects modeling found no main effect of context for the scaling component (ß=–0.07, SE = 0.05, t(117) = –1.54, p=0.13, 95% CI [-0.16 to 0.02]).
claims.source: Linear mixed effects modeling found a main effect of context for the asymmetry component (ß=–0.04, SE = 0.02, t(117) = –2.32, p=0.02, 95% CI [-0.07 to –0.01]; Figure 3c, Appendix 7—table 11), but not for the scaling component (ß=–0.07, SE = 0.05, t(117) = –1.54, p=0.13, 95% CI [-0.16 to 0.02]; Figure 3c, Appendix 7—table 12).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear mixed effects model analysis of learning rate components shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: The average asymmetry of learning rates was positive in both groups but significantly smaller in participants tested during the pandemic than those tested outside (t(121) = 2.00, p=0.048, Cohen's d=0.36).
claims.source: The average asymmetry of learning rates was positive in both groups but significantly smaller in participants tested during the pandemic than those tested outside (t(121) = 2.00, p=0.048, Cohen's d=0.36, two-sampled, two-tailed t-test, Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the t-test analysis of the asymmetry parameter shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: Participants considered positive estimation errors more than negative ones but less when experiencing the COVID-19 pandemic.
claims.source: This result indicated that participants considered positive estimation errors more than negative ones but less when experiencing the COVID-19 pandemic.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the asymmetry parameter findings.

claims.claim: In the within-subject group (n=28), there was a significant main effect of context on asymmetry (ß=–0.06, SE = 0.02, t(51) = –3.72, p=0.001, 95% CI [-0.09 to –0.03]).
claims.source: Similar results were found in the within-subject group (n=28), with a significant main effect of context on asymmetry (ß=–0.06, SE = 0.02, t(51) = –3.72, p=0.001, 95% CI [-0.09 to –0.03]; Appendix 7—table 13), but not on scaling (ß=–0.10, SE = 0.05, t(51) = –1.96, p=0.06, 95% CI [-0.21 to 0.003]; Appendix 7—table 14).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the within-subject analysis of learning rate components.

claims.claim: In the within-subject group (n=28), there was no significant main effect of context on scaling (ß=–0.10, SE = 0.05, t(51) = –1.96, p=0.06, 95% CI [-0.21 to 0.003]).
claims.source: Similar results were found in the within-subject group (n=28), with a significant main effect of context on asymmetry (ß=–0.06, SE = 0.02, t(51) = –3.72, p=0.001, 95% CI [-0.09 to –0.03]; Appendix 7—table 13), but not on scaling (ß=–0.10, SE = 0.05, t(51) = –1.96, p=0.06, 95% CI [-0.21 to 0.003]; Appendix 7—table 14).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the within-subject analysis of learning rate components.

claims.claim: The finding that optimistically biased belief updating faded during the pandemic favors the hypothesis that experiencing an adverse life event such as a pandemic weakens optimistic outlooks.
claims.source: The finding that optimistically biased belief updating faded during the pandemic favors the hypothesis that experiencing an adverse life event such as a pandemic weakens optimistic outlooks.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the main findings in relation to the study's hypotheses.

claims.claim: The findings align with the body of research that has explored the malleability of the optimistically biased belief updating and information integration under acute threat and stress and mood disorders such as depression.
claims.source: It further aligns with the body of research that has explored the malleability of the optimistically biased belief updating and information integration under acute threat and stress and mood disorders such as depression (Strunk et al., 2006; Garrett et al., 2014; Korn et al., 2014; Garrett et al., 2018; Kuper-Smith et al., 2020; Czekalla et al., 2021; Bottemanne et al., 2022; Globig et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with previous research supported by citations.

claims.claim: The sample tested during the pandemic considered positive, favorable information less while showing no change in negative, unfavorable information consideration.
claims.source: Notably, our sample tested during the pandemic considered positive, favorable information less while showing no change in negative, unfavorable information consideration.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings about information integration.

claims.claim: Mental health assessments during the COVID-19 pandemic indicated that anxiety, stress, paranoia, and depression levels were more prevalent in the population.
claims.source: Mental health assessments during the COVID-19 pandemic indicated that anxiety, stress, paranoia, and depression levels were more prevalent in the population (World Health Organization, 2022; Suthaharan et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The rapid spread of SARS-CoV-2 and the emergence of COVID-19 cases worldwide constitute a challenging situation that, in 5 months, has shifted from an elusive and distant threat to an immediate and drastic health and economic crisis.
claims.source: The rapid spread of SARS-CoV-2 and the emergence of COVID-19 cases worldwide constitute a challenging situation that, in 5 months, has shifted from an elusive and distant threat to an immediate and drastic health and economic crisis.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the COVID-19 pandemic context based on general knowledge.

claims.claim: Economic uncertainties, particularly during marked economic inequality and epidemics, can contribute to belief-updating fallacies reflected by the rise of conspiracy theories.
claims.source: Previous research has shown that economic uncertainties, particularly during marked economic inequality and epidemics, can contribute to belief-updating fallacies reflected by the rise of conspiracy theories (Leonard and Philippe, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The study did not collect physiological measures of stress or information about the COVID-19 infection status of participants.
claims.source: We did not collect physiological measures of stress or information about the COVID-19 infection status of participants, which precludes a direct exploration of the immediate effects of experiencing the infection on belief-updating behavior and the potential interaction with anxiety and stress levels.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the study's limitations.

claims.claim: Subjective ratings of the perceived risk of death from COVID-19 correlated negatively to the beliefs updating bias measured during the pandemic.
claims.source: Although subjective ratings of the perceived risk of death from COVID-19 correlated negatively to the beliefs updating bias measured during the pandemic, this result was obtained in a subset of participants, retrospectively (Appendix 5).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a supplementary analysis mentioned in the discussion.

claims.claim: The observed lack of optimistically biased belief updating may be interpreted as an adaptive response to the experience of an unprecedented level of uncertainty and chronic threat during a global crisis.
claims.source: The observed lack of optimistically biased belief updating may be interpreted as an adaptive response to the experience of an unprecedented level of uncertainty and chronic threat during a global crisis.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: RL-like updating models best explain belief updating in non-threatening, non-stressful, and predictable laboratory contexts.
claims.source: This finding aligns with past work, showing that RL-like updating models best explain belief updating in non-threatening, non-stressful, and predictable laboratory contexts (Kuzmanovic and Rigoux, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: RL strategies are a computationally efficient way to guide decision-making and belief formation when the environment is stable and predictable.

results.result: The study recruited 123 participants across four groups tested at different time points relative to the COVID-19 pandemic in France: before the outbreak (October 2019, n=30), during the first strict lockdown (March-April 2020, n=34), during a less strict lockdown (May 2021, n=31), and after the lift of the sanitary state of emergency (June 2022, n=28). A subset of 28 participants from the first group were retested during the first lockdown for within-subject comparisons. Sample sizes were determined by power analysis based on pilot data.
results.evaluation: The experimental design and sample composition are clearly described with appropriate detail (C2, C23-C26, C85-C92). The power analysis justification for sample sizes is provided (C93-C94), showing adequate planning. The within-subject component adds methodological rigor. The design appropriately addresses the research question about pandemic effects on belief updating.

results.result: Optimistically biased belief updating, observed before the pandemic, disappeared during the COVID-19 pandemic and re-emerged after the pandemic ended. This effect was driven by decreased belief updating following good news during the pandemic, with no significant change in updating following bad news. The interaction between estimation error valence and context was statistically significant (β=-5.54, p=0.001), though with 75% power leaving 25% risk for type II errors.
results.evaluation: The primary finding is supported by multiple converging statistical analyses (C27, C29-C34) including between-group comparisons, within-subject replication (C35), and robustness checks with alternative calculations (C36). The temporal pattern across four time points (C30-C32) strengthens the interpretation. However, the acknowledged 25% type II error risk (C28) indicates moderate statistical power, which is a limitation but does not invalidate the finding given the consistency across analyses.

results.result: During the pandemic, participants showed higher confidence in base rates, made fewer but larger positive estimation errors (overestimations), and showed no difference in negative estimation errors compared to those tested outside the pandemic. This pattern indicates participants held fewer but stronger negative future outlooks during the pandemic.
results.evaluation: The claims about confidence ratings (C37), estimation error patterns (C38-C42), and their interpretation (C43) are supported by appropriate statistical tests with significant results. The pattern is internally consistent: higher confidence in base rates combined with fewer but larger overestimations suggests a shift toward more cautious, reality-based assessments during the pandemic. The statistical evidence is robust with clear effect sizes reported.

results.result: Computational modeling revealed that belief updating outside the pandemic was best explained by an optimistic reinforcement learning model (pxp=1, Ef=0.77), while during the pandemic it was best explained by a rational Bayesian model (pxp=0.90, Ef=0.43). This pattern was replicated in within-subject comparisons.
results.evaluation: The model comparison results (C44-C45) are supported by appropriate Bayesian model selection metrics (protected exceedance probability and estimated frequency). The within-subject replication (C46) strengthens confidence in the finding. However, the interpretation depends on the validity of the computational models themselves, which the authors acknowledge as representing potential rather than definitive mechanisms (see C78). The model recovery analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) provides evidence for model identifiability.

results.result: Learning rates showed a main effect of estimation error valence and a significant interaction with context. The pandemic context reduced the asymmetry in learning rates between good and bad news, driven specifically by decreased learning from positive estimation errors, with no change in learning from negative errors.
results.evaluation: The learning rate analyses (C47-C54) provide mechanistic insight into the observed behavioral changes. The statistical evidence is robust with both between-subject and within-subject analyses. The pattern is consistent with the observed belief updating behavior, showing that the pandemic specifically affected processing of positive (good news) information. The directional specificity strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: Parameter recovery analysis confirmed the identifiability of the scaling and asymmetry components of learning rates. The pandemic context specifically reduced the asymmetry parameter (β=-0.04, p=0.02) but not the scaling parameter, indicating participants considered positive estimation errors less during the pandemic while maintaining overall learning capacity.
results.evaluation: The parameter recovery analysis (C55) validates that the model parameters are identifiable and meaningful. The specific effect on asymmetry but not scaling (C56-C57, C60-C61) provides mechanistic clarity about what changed during the pandemic. The within-subject replication strengthens confidence. The interpretation (C59) follows logically from the parameter estimates. This decomposition of learning rate components adds important mechanistic detail to the main findings.

results.result: The study demonstrates that belief updating shifted from optimistically biased and reinforcement learning-like outside the pandemic to more rational Bayesian-like during the pandemic. This shift was characterized by reduced integration of positive information, fewer but stronger negative estimations, and increased confidence in base rates, suggesting the change was driven more by uncertainty quantification than motivational factors.
results.evaluation: This integrative result synthesizes the main findings (C3-C8, C62, C64) and offers a mechanistic interpretation (C9). The interpretation is well-supported by the convergence of behavioral, computational, and parametric analyses. The claim about uncertainty quantification versus motivational salience (C9) is a reasonable inference from the Bayesian model fit and increased confidence in base rates, though it remains somewhat speculative as the study did not directly measure these psychological constructs.

results.result: The findings align with prior research showing malleability of optimism bias under stress and threat, and suggest an adaptive shift in cognitive strategy. The shift from computationally efficient RL strategies in stable environments to Bayesian inference under uncertainty represents complementary prediction strategies for functioning under different real-life conditions.
results.evaluation: The contextualization within prior literature (C63, C72-C74, C76-C77) is well-supported by appropriate citations. The interpretation of the findings as adaptive (C70) and representing complementary strategies (C79) is reasonable given the data, though somewhat speculative. The theoretical framework linking RL to stable environments and Bayesian inference to uncertainty is supported by cited literature (C73-C74, C76-C77). However, the adaptive interpretation would be strengthened by direct measures of outcomes or fitness.

results.result: The study did not collect physiological stress measures or COVID-19 infection status, limiting direct exploration of infection effects on belief updating. A retrospective correlation between perceived COVID-19 death risk and updating bias was found in a subset of participants.
results.evaluation: These limitations (C68) are appropriately acknowledged by the authors. The retrospective correlation finding (C69) is mentioned but appropriately qualified as limited. This honest reporting of limitations is important for interpreting the scope of the findings, though it does not undermine the main results.

results.result: The study provides insight into the resilience and adaptability of belief-updating processes during and following the COVID-19 pandemic, demonstrating the malleability of human ability to anticipate the future and adapt to conditions where overly optimistic views would be harmful. However, computational modeling provides insight into potential mechanisms without confirming that humans actually use these processes.
results.evaluation: The summary claims (C80-C81) appropriately synthesize the findings and their implications. The important caveat about computational modeling (C78) is a crucial acknowledgment that the models represent potential rather than definitive mechanisms. This balanced interpretation appropriately conveys both the contributions and limitations of the computational approach. The claims about adaptability and malleability are well-supported by the temporal pattern of results.

results.result: The belief updating task comprised 40 trials with adverse life events and base rates taken from published work. Base rates were approximately uniformly distributed (W=0.952, p=0.088), ranged from 10-70% (mean=40%), and the rating scale (3-77%) ensured adequate space for belief updating. Statistical models controlled for estimation error magnitude.
results.evaluation: The task design is clearly described (C95-C99) with appropriate methodological details and citations to prior work (C96, C99). The statistical control for estimation error magnitude (C100) is an important methodological strength. The use of established stimuli from prior research enhances comparability. The distribution check (C97) confirms appropriate stimulus properties.

results.result: The study received ethical approval from the Local Ethics Committee of Sorbonne University, all participants provided informed consent and consent to publish, and the protocol followed the Declaration of Helsinki.
results.evaluation: The ethical procedures (C82-C84) are appropriately documented and meet standard requirements for human subjects research. This is important for research integrity but represents standard practice rather than a substantive finding.

results.result: The introduction establishes that optimistically biased belief updating is important for mental health and resilience, involves asymmetric learning from positive and negative information following RL or Bayesian principles, and can be reduced by contextual factors like stress and depression. The COVID-19 pandemic represented a chronic adverse context that increased stress, anxiety, and depression.
results.evaluation: These background claims (C1, C10-C22) are appropriately supported by citations to prior literature. They establish the theoretical framework and rationale for the study. The characterization of the pandemic context (C16-C18) is well-supported. These claims represent accurate summaries of prior knowledge rather than new findings from this study.

results.result: Mental health assessments showed increased anxiety, stress, paranoia, and depression during the pandemic. The rapid spread of SARS-CoV-2 created a challenging situation that shifted from distant threat to immediate crisis. Economic uncertainties during epidemics can contribute to belief-updating fallacies.
results.evaluation: These contextual claims (C65-C67) are supported by appropriate citations and provide important background for interpreting the findings. They represent accurate characterizations of the pandemic context based on prior research rather than new findings from this study.

results.result: The primary finding that optimistically biased belief updating disappeared during the COVID-19 pandemic compared to outside the pandemic, driven by reduced updating from good news but not bad news, and that this bias re-emerged after the lift of the sanitary state of emergency. This was demonstrated through linear mixed effects models showing significant interaction effects and supported by both between-subjects and within-subjects analyses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this as the primary claim, stating the authors 'find that belief updating becomes less optimistically biased during COVID-19 compared to before it' and that they have 'generated convincing evidence for their primary claim that the pandemic significantly impacted people's belief updating away from optimistic belief updating.' The editor notes this is an 'important study' addressing how the pandemic changed belief updating.

results.result: The computational modeling result that belief updating outside the pandemic was best explained by an optimistically biased RL-like model (pxp = 1, Ef = 0.77), while during the pandemic it was best explained by a rational Bayesian updating model (pxp = 0.90, Ef = 0.43). This pattern held in both between-subjects and within-subjects analyses.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the computational modeling approach as a strength ('leveraging new RL-inspired computational approaches'), one reviewer raises concerns about model distinguishability, noting 'it is difficult to tell from the figure...how much of a divergence this is and how distinctive a pattern relative to the other models' and suggests 'the interpretation could be improved further by a clearer sense of the behavioural signatures of each model.' This indicates uncertainty about the strength of evidence distinguishing the two model families.

results.result: The learning rate analysis showing that all participants had lower learning rates for bad news than good news, but this asymmetry was significantly reduced during the pandemic, driven by decreased learning rates from positive estimation errors (t(121) = 2.17, p=0.03, Cohen's d=0.39) with no difference in learning rates from negative estimation errors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognize this as a key finding, noting 'the RL model provides evidence that learning was asymmetrically positively biased outside of the pandemic but symmetric during it (as a result of reduced learning rates from good news estimation errors).' This is presented as one of the important ways the work extends previous findings.

results.result: The parameter recovery and decomposition analysis showing successful recovery of scaling and asymmetry components, with a significant main effect of context on the asymmetry component (β=-0.04, p=0.02) but not the scaling component, indicating participants considered positive estimation errors more than negative ones but less during the pandemic.
results.evaluation: Reviewers commend the authors for adding model recovery results, stating 'The authors have added model recovery results' and noting 'there is no confusion between families of models (RL models don't get confused with Bayesian models and vice versa), which is reassuring.' This indicates acceptance of the parameter recovery methodology and findings.

results.result: The finding that experiencing the COVID-19 pandemic influenced participants' confidence in base rates, with significantly higher confidence ratings observed among those tested during the pandemic compared to outside it (β=14.11, SE = 4.52, t(233) = 3.12, p=0.002).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly critique this finding, and it is presented as part of the comprehensive characterization of belief updating changes. The editor notes the authors have 'generated convincing evidence' for pandemic impacts on belief updating, which would encompass this confidence rating finding.

results.result: The estimation error analysis showing that participants during the pandemic overestimated their risk more largely than those outside the pandemic (t(121) = -3.01, p=0.003, Cohen's d=-0.54), overestimated less frequently (t(121) = 2.40, p=0.02, Cohen's d=0.43), but showed no difference in magnitude or frequency of underestimations, indicating fewer but stronger negative future outlooks during the pandemic.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recognize this as an important extension of previous work, noting 'the reduction in optimistic updating here arises due to reduced updating from positive information (previously, in the case of environmental threat, this reduction mainly arose from increased sensitivity to negative information).' This indicates acceptance of the estimation error pattern findings.

results.result: The statistical robustness of the main interaction effect (estimation error valence by context: β=-5.54, SE = 1.69, t(232) = -3.28, p=0.001), which held across multiple analytical approaches including within-subjects analysis, alternative EE calculations, and had 75% power, though leaving a 25% risk for type II errors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly commend the power analysis, stating 'the authors are commended for doing power analyses, showing their sensitivity, and recognizing the limitations of their study' and 'the authors conduct a power analysis to show that the sample sizes are appropriate.' The editor acknowledges 'sample sizes are, by necessity, on the smaller side' but accepts the authors' handling of this limitation.

results.result: The interpretation that the fading of optimistically biased belief updating during the pandemic represents an adaptive response to uncertainty and chronic threat, driven more by quantifying uncertainty than motivational salience of optimistic outlooks, aligning with previous research on malleability of optimism bias under stress and threat.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note interpretive limitations, with the editor stating 'it remains unclear which psychological factor impacted by the pandemic drives the group differences' and one reviewer noting 'a major impediment to the interpreting the findings pertains to the lack of additional measures.' The authors are praised for taking 'great care to caveat that the findings cannot directly attribute the observed lack of optimistically biased belief updating during lockdown to psychological causes such as heightened anxiety and stress.'

results.result: The acknowledged limitation that the study did not collect physiological measures of stress or COVID-19 infection status, though subjective ratings of perceived risk of death from COVID-19 correlated negatively with belief updating bias in a subset of participants retrospectively.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognize this limitation, with one stating 'a major impediment to the interpreting the findings pertains to the lack of additional measures' and noting 'information on, for example, risk perception or need for social interaction were collected from participants during the pandemic, the fact that these could not be included in the analysis hindered the interpretation of findings.' The authors are commended for acknowledging this limitation.

results.result: The experimental design involving 123 participants (after exclusions) tested across four time points: before the pandemic (October 2019, n=30), during strict lockdown (March-April 2020, n=34), during partial lockdown (May 2021, n=31), and after lift of emergency (June 2022, n=28), with 28 participants tested both before and during the pandemic for within-subjects analysis. Sample sizes were determined by power analysis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support the methodological approach, stating 'the study uses a well-validated task, and the authors conduct a power analysis to show that the sample sizes are appropriate' and 'the authors test that their results hold in both a between-group analysis (the focus of the main paper) and a within-group analysis (mainly in the supplemental).' The editor acknowledges sample size limitations but commends the power analysis.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on experimental design and sample composition (C2, C23-C26, C85-C94). Both evaluations support the methodological approach, with peer reviewers explicitly commending the power analysis and well-validated task design that OpenEval also highlights as strengths.

Both address model comparison results (C44-C46). OpenEval finds the evidence supported with appropriate caveats about model validity, while peer reviewers express uncertainty about model distinguishability, requesting clearer behavioral signatures to differentiate models. This represents a notable disagreement in confidence level.

Perfect agreement on parameter recovery analysis (C55-C61). Both evaluations support the methodology and findings, with peer reviewers explicitly noting reassurance that model families are not confused and OpenEval highlighting the mechanistic clarity provided by the parameter decomposition.

Complete alignment on study limitations (C68-C69). Both evaluations acknowledge the lack of additional psychological measures and limited retrospective correlations. Peer reviewers commend the authors for transparent acknowledgment, matching OpenEval's assessment of appropriate limitation reporting.

Strong agreement on learning rate analyses (C47-C48, C51-C54). Both evaluations support the finding that asymmetric learning changed during the pandemic due to reduced good news learning rates. Peer reviewers recognize this as an important extension of previous work.

Both address estimation error patterns (C38-C43 vs C38-C43, C7). OpenEval and peer reviewers support these findings, with peer reviewers noting this represents an important distinction from prior work on environmental threat, where changes arose from increased sensitivity to negative information.

Both address the primary finding of reduced optimistic bias (C29-C34 overlap). OpenEval supports the finding with caveats about moderate power, while peer reviewers provide unqualified support, stating the authors generated 'convincing evidence' for this primary claim. Minor difference in emphasis on statistical power concerns.

Partial overlap on statistical methodology (C27-C28, C35-C36). Both evaluations support the analytical approach. Peer reviewers explicitly commend the power analysis and sensitivity testing, while OpenEval notes the 25% type II error risk as a limitation but finds the evidence sufficient given consistency across analyses.

Both address interpretation and mechanisms (C62, C64, C9 overlap). OpenEval supports the interpretation with caveats about speculation, while peer reviewers express uncertainty, noting 'it remains unclear which psychological factor impacted by the pandemic drives the group differences.' Peer reviewers emphasize interpretive limitations more strongly.

Partial overlap on primary claims (C3-C5). OpenEval's integrative result synthesizes main findings including reduced optimistic bias, while peer reviewers focus specifically on this as the primary claim with strong support. Both are supportive but address different scopes.

Both address contextualization and interpretation (C63, C70 overlap). OpenEval supports the theoretical framework with citations while noting adaptive interpretation is somewhat speculative. Peer reviewers express greater uncertainty about psychological mechanisms, emphasizing the lack of additional measures as a 'major impediment' to interpretation.

Minimal overlap on confidence ratings (C37). OpenEval provides detailed support for confidence and estimation error findings, while peer reviewers briefly acknowledge this without explicit critique as part of the comprehensive evidence for pandemic impacts.
